# Team Science for Biostatisticians {#sec-team-science}

The first email from Dr. X, a cardiologist, is four lines long.
The hospital's data warehouse holds about five thousand
heart-failure discharges; some patients had a home-health visit
within a week and some did not; could you 'run the numbers'
showing that the visits cut 30-day readmissions, in time for an
abstract due next month? As posed, the comparison has a flaw no
software will report: a patient readmitted on day 3 never had
the chance of a day-5 visit, so the sickest patients are counted
as unvisited, and home health looks protective whether or not it
does anything. The analysis would run, the estimate would be
precise, and the paper would be wrong. What prevents it is not a
better model but a conversation, held before any code, that this
chapter follows from that email to the HF-HOME trial whose plan,
data, and report the rest of the book uses.

::: {.bookepigraph}
```{=latex}
\begin{flushright}\small
```
*The best thing about being a statistician is that you get
to play in everyone's backyard.*

[John W. Tukey]{.smallcaps}, attributed; quoted in his
*New York Times* obituary (2000)
```{=latex}
\end{flushright}
```
:::

## Where you sit: the collaboration spectrum {#sec-team-science-roles}

Most biostatisticians spend the greater part of their careers on
teams alongside people who cannot read their code and do not
share their vocabulary. Working across that gap is a learned
skill, not a personality trait, and the distinction matters
because skills can be taught. A statistician described as
'difficult to work with' has usually not been rude to anyone.
They have failed to establish, in writing and early, what was
being asked and what would be delivered, and every later
disagreement has been argued without a shared record of what was
agreed. That is the shape of nearly every collaboration failure
in this chapter: not a clash of personalities but an absent
document.

The first thing to establish is the role. An investigator who
says 'we need a statistician' may be asking for a methodological
consult, a hands-on collaborator, a co-investigator on the grant,
or hired labor for the analysis section of a manuscript. The
expectations, the timeline, the authorship implications, and the
appropriate level of pushback differ for each
(@tbl-team-science-spectrum).

| Position | Mode | Your role | Authorship expectation | Where it is common |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Consultant | Transactional: a question or dataset arrives, an answer leaves | Analysis or methodological advice | Usually acknowledgment; the deliverable is the analysis or report | Statistical consulting services, industry consulting groups |
| Collaborator | Sustained across design, analysis, and writing | Substantively involved in the science | Authorship when the ICMJE criteria are met (@sec-team-science-authorship) | Most academic biostatistics |
| Co-investigator | Named on the grant, with allocated effort | Partial authority over direction; deeply involved in design | Authorship, and effort paid from the grant | Mid-career and senior statisticians on funded research |
| Principal investigator (PI) | Leads the project | The statistical method is itself the science | First or last author | Methodological research; less common as lead in clinical research |

: The collaboration spectrum. Authority, time, and credit rise
together down the table. {#tbl-team-science-spectrum}

The common source of tension is mismatch: a statistician treated
as a consultant who sees themselves as a collaborator, or the
reverse. Dr. X's email reads like a consulting request ('run the
numbers'), but the question inside it, whether home health
changes outcomes, needs a collaborator from design onward.
Naming the position out loud at intake is the first step in
avoiding the mismatch.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Dr. X offers to list you in the acknowledgments
'for the stats'. You expect to design the analysis, write the
methods and results, and revise the manuscript. Where on the
spectrum is each of you placing the engagement, and when should
the difference be raised?

**Answer.** Dr. X is describing a consultant; the work you
expect is a collaborator's, which carries authorship when the
ICMJE criteria are met. Raise it at intake, before any analysis
runs, and record the agreement in the scope of work
(@sec-team-science-sow). Raised at submission, the same
conversation is a dispute about work already done.
:::

## The intake conversation {#sec-team-science-intake}

The first meeting with a new collaborator sets the trajectory of
the collaboration, and it does so mostly through what is not
asked. An investigator arrives with a dataset and a question, the
statistician takes the work, and the terms nobody raised (what
the deliverable is, when it is due, whether there will be
authorship) become assumptions that each party holds privately
and differently. They surface months later, during the only week
in which everyone is busy.

The remedy is a structured intake, which is less formal than it
sounds: a fixed set of questions asked in the first conversation
and written down afterward (@tbl-team-science-intake). Sending
the questions before the meeting often resolves half the issues
without the meeting.

| Topic | What to ask | What the answer decides |
|---|---|---|
| The scientific question | What are you trying to find out, and what would the answer enable? Push past 'is A better than B' to 'better in what sense, for which patients, in what setting' | The design |
| The data | What exists; how it was collected; what can be shared; whether it exists yet | Most of the project's fate |
| The deadline | A grant deadline in three months, or an exploratory question with none? | What is feasible |
| Authorship | Co-author, acknowledgment, or hired help? | The position on the spectrum |
| The deliverables | A two-page memo, a Quarto report, a paper, a regulatory submission? | The time commitment |
| Approvals | Which institutional review board (IRB) protocol and which data use agreement (DUA) cover this use? | Whether the work may start |

: The intake questions. Write the answers down the same day.
{#tbl-team-science-intake}

### Red flags

Some answers warrant more questions before you agree to
anything:

- A request to perform a specific test ('we want a chi-square')
  without the hypothesis it is meant to test.
- A dataset the team has already analyzed several times ('it
  didn't show what we hoped'), which makes any hypothesis now
  proposed a post hoc one.
- A comparison defined by what patients received after the
  starting point, which builds in immortal time.
- Pressure to produce results by next week.
- Vague answers about the IRB protocol or the DUA.

Dr. X's email carries three of these: a fixed answer in search of
an analysis ('showing that the visits cut readmissions'), a
deadline, and an exposure defined by what happened after
discharge.

### Worked example: the intake document

The document below is what the intake conversation with Dr. X
produced, for a cohort drawn from the electronic health record
(EHR). It reframes the question with a landmark, so that every
patient's exposure is fixed before follow-up begins, and it lists
the red flags that remain.

> **Project.** Post-discharge home health visits and 30-day
> readmission or death in heart-failure patients.
>
> **Investigator.** Dr. X, Cardiology.
>
> **Question.** Among heart-failure patients alive and not
> readmitted 7 days after discharge (the landmark), is receiving
> at least one home health visit in those 7 days associated with
> lower all-cause readmission or death over days 8 to 30, after
> adjustment for measured confounders?
>
> **Data.** Retrospective EHR cohort, $n \approx 5{,}000$,
> obtained from the institutional research data warehouse under
> existing IRB. Includes demographics, baseline ejection
> fraction, medication on discharge, date of each home health
> visit (needed for the landmark), dates of readmission and
> death.
>
> **Deadline.** Manuscript draft by month 4; submit month 6.
>
> **Methodology (to be confirmed).** Propensity-matched cohort
> with multivariable logistic regression for the primary
> outcome. Sensitivity analyses with inverse-probability
> weighting.
>
> **Deliverables.** Pre-registered analysis plan (month 1), Table
> 1 and primary results (month 2), manuscript draft (month 4),
> revisions (month 5).
>
> **Authorship.** Statistician will be second author. Will be
> involved in writing methods and results, and revising the full
> manuscript.
>
> **Boundaries.** Statistician will not write the introduction or
> discussion. Statistician will not perform additional analyses
> requested after month 4 without renegotiation.
>
> **Red flags noted.** (1) Immortal time: as first posed ('a
> visit within 7 days' against a 30-day outcome), patients
> readmitted before a visit could happen would count as
> unexposed, flattering home health. Addressed by the 7-day
> landmark above. (2) Confounding by indication: referral for
> home health depends on frailty and social support, which the
> EHR records poorly; propensity methods adjust only for what is
> measured, so the result is an association, and a causal answer
> needs a randomized trial. (3) Outcome capture: admissions
> elsewhere are missed unless the EHR is linked to the state
> health-information exchange. (4) Deaths before readmission are
> counted in the outcome, not treated as non-events. To revisit
> if EHR data quality is worse than expected at first
> exploration.

The document did its job twice.
It removed the immortal time from the question, and its second
red flag told Dr. X what the cohort could not deliver: if the
question is whether home health *causes* fewer readmissions, the
answer needs randomization. That is the decision that turned this
project into HF-HOME, the randomized trial whose statistical
analysis plan (SAP) is the worked example of @sec-analysis-plan.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Read your intake document as a stranger would, and confirm that
each row of @tbl-team-science-intake has an answer in it that a
third party could check: a named question, a named data source
and approval, dates, an authorship statement, deliverables, and
every red flag with what was done about it. A blank or a 'to be
discussed' is a disagreement scheduled for later.
:::

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
A model is a useful second reader for a request, provided you
write your own list first.

> **Context.** I am a biostatistician. Below is an email from a
> clinical collaborator asking for an analysis. [paste the email,
> with names, dates, and any data removed]
>
> **Constraints.** Do not propose an analysis. Do not soften the
> list for tone. Consider at least: a test named without a
> hypothesis, a hypothesis formed after looking at the data,
> exposure defined after the start of follow-up (immortal time),
> confounding by indication, deadline pressure, missing approvals
> (IRB, DUA), how the data would be transferred, and the
> authorship offered against the work requested.
>
> **Criteria.** Return a table: the quoted phrase, the red flag,
> why it matters, and the question I should ask. Mark any flag
> you are unsure of as uncertain.

*Failure mode.* Models flag the explicit issues (no IRB, no
analysis plan, vague hypotheses) and miss the subtle ones: a
dataset the team has silently inspected, so that the 'hypothesis'
is post hoc, and an exposure that can only occur among patients
who survived long enough to receive it. *Check.* Compare the
table with the list you wrote before prompting, and with the
model answer to exercise 1 below; any flag on neither list goes
to a senior colleague before the reply is sent. The email may go
to the model only after you have removed patient information
(@sec-ai-governance).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Why does the intake document name a 7-day landmark
instead of comparing patients with and without 'a visit within 7
days'?

**Answer.** Exposure must be fixed before follow-up starts. A
patient readmitted or dead on day 3 could not have had a day-5
visit, so the naive comparison counts the sickest patients as
unexposed and makes home health look protective. Starting
follow-up at day 7, among patients still alive and not
readmitted, assigns every patient's exposure before any outcome
is counted. @sec-analysis-plan meets the same trap inside the
trial, where an event before the planned visit erases the visit.
:::

### Exercises

1. After HF-HOME reports, Dr. X sends a second email. List every
   red flag in it, say what each threatens, and draft a reply of
   no more than six sentences.

   > Hi, the trial came back not significant, which was a
   > surprise. The team has been going through the data and the
   > patients who actually got the home visit did much better
   > than usual care. Could you run a quick chi-square on just
   > those patients versus usual care? The abstract deadline is
   > Friday. I'll email you the spreadsheet from my laptop. Happy
   > to thank you in the acknowledgments!

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
| Phrase | Red flag | What it threatens |
|---|---|---|
| 'the team has been going through the data' | The hypothesis was formed after looking at the outcomes | Any p-value from the new comparison is uninterpretable |
| 'the patients who actually got the home visit' | An as-treated subset of one randomized arm | Randomization: patients who received the visit differ from those who did not, and patients with early events could not receive it (immortal time) |
| 'a quick chi-square' | A test named without a hypothesis or estimand | The design dictating nothing and the test dictating everything |
| 'deadline is Friday' | Deadline pressure | Time for a correct analysis or a considered refusal |
| 'email you the spreadsheet from my laptop' | Trial data held and transferred outside the approved system | The data use and security terms of the protocol |
| 'thank you in the acknowledgments' | Authorship offered without reference to the work | ICMJE eligibility, which depends on the work, not the offer |

A reply that holds the line: 'Thanks; I know the result was
disappointing. The comparison of visited patients with usual care
is not one I can run as a test of home health, because the
patients who received a visit differ from those who did not in
ways randomization no longer balances, including that patients
with early readmissions never had the chance of a visit. The
trial's answer is the as-randomized comparison, and I can help
write it up as an informative inconclusive result by Friday. If
the team wants the visited-patient analysis, I can run it as a
labeled exploratory analysis with appropriate adjustment, after
the abstract. Please do not send trial data by email; I will pull
it from the trial's analysis environment.' The first flag is the
one most readers miss, because the email presents it as
observation rather than as analysis.
:::

## The scope of work {#sec-team-science-sow}

For any non-trivial collaboration, a written scope of work (SOW)
turns the intake into commitments. It is not a legal contract; it
is a shared understanding. When the project drifts, as projects
do, the SOW is the document everyone returns to, and the document
is what you defend when expectations diverge. Verbal agreements
about scope, deadlines, authorship, and analytic decisions
evaporate; send an email summary after every meeting, and write
the analysis plan before any analysis runs (Habit 5).
@tbl-team-science-sow is a template, filled in for the HF-HOME
trial that grew out of Dr. X's intake.

| Element | What to write | HF-HOME example |
|---|---|---|
| Inputs | What the collaborator provides, by when, in what format | Randomization list and case report form (CRF) exports from the trial's data management system, monthly from first enrollment |
| Outputs | What you produce, by when | Locked SAP before the first outcome is ascertained; Table 1 and primary analysis within six weeks of database lock; methods and results sections of the main paper |
| Methodology | The high-level approach, and where it will be pre-specified | As-randomized comparison of 30-day readmission or death; full detail in the SAP (@sec-analysis-plan) |
| Revisions | How many rounds are included; what counts as a major change | Two rounds of manuscript revision; a new outcome, population, or model is a renegotiation |
| Authorship and acknowledgment | As agreed at intake, against the ICMJE criteria | Statistician is an author on the main paper and on any secondary paper using the trial's analysis; contributions recorded in CRediT terms |
| Boundaries | What you will *not* do | No introduction or discussion; no analyses added after database lock without an SAP amendment; no work on data outside the approved environment |

: A scope-of-work template, with the HF-HOME entries.
{#tbl-team-science-sow}

The boundaries row is the one most often left blank and most
often needed. It is where 'one more quick analysis' gets an
answer that was written before anyone was annoyed.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Two months after database lock, Dr. X asks for a
subgroup analysis by ejection-fraction stratum for a conference.
Which rows of the SOW govern the request, and what do they tell
you to do?

**Answer.** Boundaries (no analyses added after lock without an
SAP amendment) and Revisions (a new analysis is a
renegotiation). Neither says no. They say the analysis is
exploratory unless the SAP pre-specified it, that it must be
labeled as such, and that the time it takes is a new commitment
to be agreed, not absorbed. A subgroup the SAP did name is
already in scope.
:::

### Exercises

2. Each request below arrives during HF-HOME. Name the SOW row
   that governs it and say whether it is in scope.
   (a) A reviewer asks for the primary analysis adjusted for
   site. (b) Dr. X asks you to draft the discussion section.
   (c) A site coordinator offers to send you an updated CRF
   export as an email attachment. (d) Dr. X asks for a second
   paper on 90-day mortality.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
(a) Revisions and Methodology: in scope if the SAP names site as
a stratification factor, as HF-HOME's does, since adjusting for
stratification factors is standard; a response to a reviewer is
one of the agreed revision rounds. (b) Boundaries: out of scope;
you may comment on the discussion, but drafting it is the
investigators' work unless renegotiated. (c) Inputs and
Boundaries: out of scope as offered, because inputs come from the
trial's data management system and you do not work on data
outside the approved environment; ask for the export through the
agreed route. (d) Outputs and Authorship: a new paper with a new
outcome is a new scope of work, with its own analysis plan and
its own authorship agreement, even though the data are the same.
:::

## Handling disagreement {#sec-team-science-disagreement}

Not every methodological choice is worth a confrontation, and
distinguishing preference from principle is what makes you a
useful collaborator rather than a pedantic one. When you and a
collaborator disagree, the response depends on what is at stake
(@tbl-team-science-tiers).

| Tier | What it covers | HF-HOME example | Your response |
|---|---|---|---|
| Preference | Coding style, the reference level of a factor, plotting choices, the order of a table | Dr. X wants usual care as the second column of Table 1 | Defer, unless there is a substantive reason not to |
| Best practice | Multiplicity correction, intention-to-treat analysis, missing-data handling, sensitivity analyses | Dr. X wants to drop the tipping-point analysis of unascertained outcomes to save space | Argue for the standard; if overruled, record the dissent in the SAP or the methods |
| Validity | An inappropriate test, data dredging, a hypothesis chosen after seeing the data, dichotomizing a continuous outcome, comparisons that break randomization | Dr. X wants the visited patients compared with usual care as the trial's result | Push back firmly; if the analysis is still methodologically wrong, withdraw from it |

: Three tiers of disagreement and the response to each.
{#tbl-team-science-tiers}

The middle tier is where most disagreements live and where
judgment is most consequential. Picking too many fights makes you
a difficult collaborator; picking none makes you complicit in bad
analyses. Withdrawing, at the third tier, means declining to put
your name or your analysis to the result, said plainly and once;
@sec-ethics catalogs the cases where it is warranted.

### Talking about results

How you report a result to a collaborator is the subject of
@sec-communicating, which owns the memo, the talk, and the
response to reviewers. Three points belong here, because they
come up in every collaboration before anything is written.

**Report the quantity the listener will act on.** That is an
effect size with its uncertainty, not a p-value: 'the treatment
reduced HbA1c (glycated hemoglobin) by 0.6 percentage points (95%
confidence interval [CI] 0.3 to 0.9)' says more than 'the effect
was significant at p < 0.001', which is the p-value that interval
implies. In a meeting, lead with the conclusion and give the
support if asked; in a paper, write the conclusion in plain
language and include the quantitative support.

**Match the verb to the evidence** (Habit 11). The three
registers in @tbl-team-science-verbs are different claims, and
@sec-communicating and @sec-ethics build on them.

| Register | What it claims | When the evidence supports it |
|---|---|---|
| 'We found X' | X is established by this study | The interval excludes no effect, and the design licenses the verb |
| 'The data are consistent with X' | X is among the values the data support | X lies inside the interval, along with other values |
| 'We cannot rule out X' | X has not been excluded | X lies inside the interval, and so does no effect |

: Three registers of a claim. An inconclusive trial such as
HF-HOME supports the second and third, not the first.
{#tbl-team-science-verbs}

**Say which kind of interval it is.** 'For 60-year-old patients
with baseline HbA1c of 8%, the model estimates an average of about
7.4% under treatment (95% CI 7.1 to 7.7%)' describes the *average*
patient like this; a single patient's value is far less certain.
With a residual standard deviation of 0.6 points, the 95%
prediction interval for one such patient runs from about 6.2 to
8.6%, and a clinician who reads the narrower interval as a
forecast for the patient in front of them has been misinformed.

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**A disagreement settled by phone leaves no record, and the
analysis that ships is the one you objected to.** When you are
overruled on a best-practice question, the dissent exists only if
it is written: an SAP amendment, a sentence in the methods, or at
minimum an email summary sent the same day. Without it, the
choice reads later as yours.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Dr. X proposes reporting HF-HOME's primary outcome
as 'home health reduced readmission or death', citing the point
estimate. Which tier is the disagreement, and which register does
the result support?

**Answer.** Validity: the sentence claims an effect the interval
does not establish, which misrepresents the result. HF-HOME's
interval includes no effect, so the result supports 'the data are
consistent with a modest reduction' and 'we cannot rule out no
effect', and the plain summary is that the trial was
inconclusive. @sec-communicating works the memo through with the
computed numbers.
:::

### Exercises

3. Classify each request as preference, best practice, or
   validity, and give your response in one sentence. (a) Report
   odds ratios rather than risk differences in a secondary table.
   (b) Dichotomize N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide
   (NT-proBNP) at its median 'to make the result
   easier to explain' in a press release. (c) Omit the
   adjustment for multiple secondary outcomes. (d) Use a
   different color palette for the figures.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
(a) Preference, provided the primary estimand (a risk difference
in HF-HOME) is reported as pre-specified: defer, and suggest the
risk difference beside the odds ratio for readers. (b) Validity:
dichotomizing a continuous measure discards information, makes
the result depend on an arbitrary cut, and here serves a press
release; decline, and offer a plain-language statement of the
continuous result instead. (c) Best practice: argue for the
pre-specified procedure, and if overruled, state in the methods
that no adjustment was made and label the secondary results
exploratory. (d) Preference: defer, checking only that the
palette is legible to color-blind readers.
:::

## Authorship and credit {#sec-team-science-authorship}

Authorship allocates credit in an academic system where credit
allocates grants, promotions, and standing, and unresolved
authorship disputes sour collaborations and sometimes end them.
The ICMJE defines authorship by four criteria, all four of which must be
met [@icmje2024]:

1. Substantial contributions to the conception or design of the
   work; or the acquisition, analysis, or interpretation of data.
2. Drafting the work or revising it critically for important
   intellectual content.
3. Final approval of the version to be published.
4. Agreement to be accountable for all aspects of the work.

The ICMJE also asks that anyone who meets the first criterion be
given the opportunity to meet the other three, by taking part in
drafting, review, and approval. Contributors who do not qualify,
including those whose only role was funding, general supervision,
or administrative support, are acknowledged.

**CRediT is a separate question.** CRediT describes *what* each
contributor did, in fourteen named roles such as
Conceptualization, Formal analysis, Data curation, and Writing –
review & editing [@brand2015beyond]. It does not decide *who* is
an author; the ICMJE criteria do. A contributor can hold several
CRediT roles and still not be an author, and a journal that asks
for a CRediT statement is asking for a description, not a ruling.
@tbl-team-science-authorship applies both to the HF-HOME main
paper.

| Contributor | ICMJE 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | Decision | CRediT roles |
|---|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|---|---|
| Lead statistician: wrote the SAP, ran the analysis, drafted the methods and results, approved the final version | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Author | Methodology; Formal analysis; Software; Writing – original draft |
| Co-analyst: independently reprogrammed the primary analysis; has not yet seen the manuscript | Yes | Not yet | Not yet | Not yet | Offer drafting and approval; author if all four are then met | Validation; Software |
| Site coordinator: enrolled patients and collected the CRF data; reviewed and approved the manuscript | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Author | Investigation; Data curation |
| Department chair: secured the funding; no other role | No | No | No | No | Acknowledge | Funding acquisition |
| Statistician who answered one design question by email | No | No | No | No | Acknowledge | None as an author |
| Statistician who ran a test for an abstract and never saw the abstract | Yes | No | No | No | Acknowledge, unless offered and accepting a role in drafting and approval | Formal analysis |

: Authorship scenarios for the HF-HOME main paper. ICMJE decides
the 'Decision' column; CRediT only describes.
{#tbl-team-science-authorship}

In practice the lead statistician on a clinical trial is
routinely an author; a statistician who wrote the analysis but
did not see the manuscript before submission is in a weak
position, because criteria 3 and 4 cannot be met after the fact.
Discussing authorship at the start of the project, in writing,
prevents the confrontation at submission.

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
A model can draft a contribution statement; it cannot decide
authorship.

> **Context.** Below are the contributors to a manuscript and, for
> each, a factual list of what they did. The authorship list has
> already been decided against the ICMJE criteria. [paste names
> and contributions]
>
> **Constraints.** Use only the fourteen CRediT role names,
> spelled as the taxonomy spells them. Do not add, remove, or
> reorder authors, and do not comment on who should be an author.
> Assign a role only when a listed contribution supports it.
>
> **Criteria.** Return a table of author and roles, then the
> statement in the journal's format. Flag any author with no
> supported role.

*Failure mode.* The model assigns generous roles (Conceptualization
for everyone, Writing for anyone who commented) or vague ones
('contributed to the project'), which is how ghost and gift
authorship look on paper; asked a question about authorship, it
answers with CRediT roles as if they settled it. *Check.* Confirm
every role name against the CRediT list, and send each author
their own line to confirm before submission; an author who cannot
confirm a role does not get it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A clinical collaborator brings you a dataset and
asks for 'a quick t-test for an abstract'. You run the test and
email back the result. The abstract is accepted with you as
second author. Is this appropriate?

**Answer.** Probably not. You meet criterion 1 (analysis of
data), but criteria 2 and 3 are unmet: you did not see the
abstract before submission, and you cannot be accountable
(criterion 4) for text you have not read. Acknowledgment is the
more defensible attribution, unless you are given, and take, the
chance to revise and approve it. The right time to settle this
was the start: 'I will do the test if I can review the abstract
before it goes in', or 'this counts as a service contribution;
please acknowledge'.
:::

### Exercises

4. For a secondary HF-HOME paper on medication burden, decide
   authorship for each contributor and give at least one CRediT
   role: (a) a pharmacist who designed the coding scheme for the
   discharge medication strings and helped draft the methods,
   and approved the paper; (b) a data manager who exported the
   files and has seen no draft; (c) Dr. X, who proposed the
   question, revised the manuscript, and approved it; (d) a
   graduate student who checked the medication coding against the
   source records and is offered, and accepts, a role in revising
   and approving the paper.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
(a) Author: design of a component of the work (criterion 1),
drafting (2), approval (3), and, by approving, accountability
(4), provided they agree to it; CRediT Methodology, Data
curation, Writing – original draft. (b) Acknowledge as things
stand: the export alone is a modest contribution to acquisition,
and criteria 2 to 4 are unmet; CRediT Data curation describes the
role whether or not they become an author. (c) Author:
Conceptualization, Writing – review & editing. (d) Author, once
all four criteria are met: the verification is a substantial
contribution to acquisition and analysis, and the ICMJE asks that
such a contributor be given the chance to meet the rest; CRediT
Validation, Writing – review & editing. The CRediT roles describe
each person in every case; the decision column comes from ICMJE.
:::

## Managing a portfolio of projects {#sec-team-science-portfolio}

The intake conversation and the scope of work govern a single
collaboration. The defining structural fact of a collaborative
biostatistician's work is that there is never only one. You will
carry five to fifteen active projects at once, at different
stages, for different investigators, each of whom is convinced
theirs is the one you are working on today. Survey evidence ranks
managing multiple simultaneous projects among the most essential
skills in the work, second only to coding for those in their
first five years [@slade2023team]. No software installs it.

**The unit of work is the portfolio, not the project.** A junior
statistician experiences the job as a queue: finish project A,
then start project B. Projects instead arrive on the
investigators' schedules, block on data and approvals you do not
control, and then unblock several at once. The competence asked
of you is to hold many partly finished projects in a legible
state and move each when it is movable, not to drive one to
completion while the rest quietly decay. @tbl-team-science-portfolio
is what a legible portfolio looks like.

| Project | Investigator | Stage | Next deliverable | Blocked on (owner) | Hours this week |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| HF-HOME main paper | Dr. X | Analysis | Primary results and Table 1 | Nothing | 12 |
| Readmission risk model | Dr. Y | Data acquisition | Cohort definition memo | Data extract (warehouse team, requested on the 3rd) | 1 |
| Sepsis registry | Dr. Z | Revision | Response to reviewers | Nothing; due in 3 weeks | 6 |
| Stroke rehabilitation pilot | Dr. W | Design | Sample-size calculation | Choice of primary outcome (Dr. W) | 1 |
| Grant resubmission | Dr. X | Writing | Statistical analysis section | Nothing; due in 5 weeks | 4 |

: A sample project portfolio, reviewed weekly. The 'Blocked on'
column names a person, not a state.
{#tbl-team-science-portfolio}

**Estimate, then double.** Statisticians are systematically
optimistic about how long an analysis takes, because the estimate
imagines the clean path and the work is mostly the mess: the
merge that reveals duplicated IDs, the outcome coded three ways
across sites, the model that will not converge. Estimate the
clean path, double it, and add the one review cycle you forgot.
Promising month 2 and delivering in month 2 builds more standing
than promising month 1 and delivering in month 3.

**Make blocking visible, to yourself and to them.** Much of a
statistician's calendar is spent waiting: for the data extract,
for the IRB amendment, for the collaborator to say which of two
outcomes is primary. A blocked project is a debt that comes due,
usually at the worst moment. For every active project, track the
single thing it is waiting on and who owns it. When a PI asks
why their analysis has not moved, 'I am waiting on the corrected
data file I requested on the 3rd' is an answer; silence is not.

**Protect the cost of re-entry.** The expensive part of juggling
projects is not the analysis but the reconstruction paid each
time you return to a project set down three weeks ago. A project
that rebuilds with one command (@sec-rrtools, @sec-zzcollab),
whose analytic decisions are fixed in an analysis plan
(@sec-analysis-plan), and whose history is legible in Git
(@sec-git-solo) can be put down and picked up in minutes; one
held together in your head and an untracked script cannot.
Reproducible infrastructure is usually justified as a courtesy to
reviewers and future replicators. Its quieter and more immediate
payoff is that it lets you carry fifteen projects without
dropping any (Habit 1).

**Batch the switches you can; price the ones you cannot.**
Context switching is not free, and the statistician who answers
every email the instant it arrives pays the re-entry cost a
hundred times a day. Where the work allows, batch it: a block for
one project's analysis, a separate block for correspondence
across all projects. A few switches are forced by genuine urgency
and earn their cost; most are not, and the skill is telling the
two apart.

**Capacity is finite, and saying so is part of the job.** The
boundaries row of the scope of work declines work within a
project. The same discipline operates across projects: a
statistician who never says 'I can start this in three weeks, not
this week' ends up doing everything late rather than some things
on time. Deferring is not a failure of collaboration; committing
to a deadline you cannot meet is.

None of this requires a particular tool. A single list like
@tbl-team-science-portfolio, reviewed once a week, is enough. The
tool is not the skill; the habit of keeping the portfolio legible
is.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** It is Monday, and four projects are active. A has a
grant deadline Friday and is waiting on nothing. B is a
manuscript revision due in three weeks, blocked on a corrected
data file that has not arrived. C is an exploratory analysis with
no deadline whose PI emailed this morning asking for an update. D
is a reviewer response due tomorrow and is half drafted. In what
order do you work, and what do you send before you start?

**Answer.** Before starting, send two messages: a reminder to B's
data owner that you remain blocked on the corrected file, and a
one-line reply to C's PI with a realistic date, because an
unanswered ask silently curdles into a grievance. Then work D
first: it is due tomorrow, and its remaining cost is the best
known because it is half done. Then A: due Friday, unblocked, and
the larger unknown, so it wants the fresh part of the day. B
cannot move until the file arrives, so the reminder was your only
move on it today. C waits until A and D are clear. The queue
model's error here is working C because its email sits on top of
the inbox.
:::

### Exercises

5. You have 20 working hours this week for project work. Your
   clean-path estimates are: HF-HOME primary results, 8 hours, due
   Friday; a sepsis-registry reviewer response, 4 hours, due in
   three weeks; a new intake meeting with Dr. V, 1 hour,
   requested for this week; a power calculation for Dr. W, 3
   hours, blocked until Dr. W chooses the primary outcome. Using
   'estimate, then double', decide what you commit to this week,
   what you defer, and what you send to whom.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
Doubled, the estimates are 16, 8, 2, and 6 hours: 32 hours of
work against 20 available, so something must be deferred, and
saying so on Monday is the job. Commit to the HF-HOME results (16
hours, due Friday) and the intake meeting (2 hours, because a new
collaborator's first impression is set by whether you make
time). That leaves 2 hours, not enough for the reviewer
response, which is due in three weeks and can start next week.
Dr. W's power calculation cannot start at all; send Dr. W a
one-line message that the calculation is waiting on the choice
of primary outcome, and offer two candidate outcomes to choose
between. Send the sepsis-registry PI a date for the response. The
schedule fits because nothing blocked was counted as work, and
nothing unblocked was promised that the doubled estimate could
not hold.
:::

## Rules of thumb

1. **Habit 5: agree in writing before the analysis runs.** The
   intake document, the scope of work, and the analysis plan are
   the record every later disagreement is settled against.
2. **Habit 11: match the verb to the design.** At intake, ask
   whether the question needs 'causes' or 'is associated with',
   and choose the design that licenses the verb you need.
3. **Habit 1: the compendium is the unit.** A project that
   rebuilds with one command is one you can set down and pick up,
   which is what makes a portfolio of fifteen possible.

## Cumulative practice

6. *Cumulative (uses @sec-why).* Midway through HF-HOME, Dr. X
   asks you to skip the analysis plan and the version-controlled
   compendium 'just this once' to make an abstract deadline.
   Write the reply, using the cost-benefit case of @sec-why and
   the rows of the scope of work that apply.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
A strong reply concedes the deadline, refuses the shortcut, and
offers what can be done. It names the cost in Dr. X's terms: an
abstract result produced outside the plan is one that cannot be
reproduced for the paper, and a number that changes between the
abstract and the paper is the event @sec-why describes. It cites
the SOW's Outputs and Boundaries rows (a locked SAP before
outcomes; no analyses outside the agreed environment), so the
refusal rests on an agreement rather than a preference. And it
offers an alternative: the pre-specified baseline table, which
needs no outcome data, or a submission at the next deadline.
:::

7. *On your own work (no key).* List every project you currently
   have active. For each, write its stage, its single next
   action, and the one thing it is blocked on, together with who
   owns that thing. Any project for which you cannot name a next
   action is the one in trouble; say why.

## Cheat sheet

| Situation | Do | Tool |
|---|---|---|
| A new request arrives | Ask the intake questions; name the position on the spectrum | @tbl-team-science-intake, @tbl-team-science-spectrum |
| The request names a test, not a question | Ask for the hypothesis and the estimand first | Red-flag list |
| Exposure is defined by what happened after the start | Fix exposure before follow-up, with a landmark or randomization | Intake document |
| The intake is done | Write the scope of work the same week | @tbl-team-science-sow |
| A collaborator disagrees | Classify the tier before responding | @tbl-team-science-tiers |
| You are overruled on best practice | Record the dissent in writing the same day | SAP amendment or methods sentence |
| Reporting a result in conversation | Effect size and interval first; match the verb | @tbl-team-science-verbs |
| Deciding authorship | ICMJE decides; CRediT describes | @tbl-team-science-authorship |
| Too many projects | Double the estimates; name every block and its owner | @tbl-team-science-portfolio |

: Team science at a glance. {#tbl-team-science-cheat-sheet}

## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-03}

1. Consulting is typically transactional: a question is
   brought, a statistical analysis is delivered, and the
   relationship ends. Collaboration is sustained: the
   statistician is a team member involved across study design,
   data collection, analysis, and manuscript writing, and shares
   authorship responsibility for the final product. The middle
   ground (a few sustained interactions that do not span the
   whole project) is where most role disputes happen.
2. Active listening (understanding the scientific question
   before proposing a method), precise writing (producing
   analysis plans and memos that non-statisticians can audit),
   and calibrated language (distinguishing 'verified', 'likely',
   'assumed', and 'unknown' in reports). Many biostatisticians'
   technical skill outpaces their communication; the gap shows up
   as 'difficult to work with'.
3. Authorship determines credit in an academic system where
   credit allocates grants, promotions, and prestige. Unresolved
   authorship disputes sour collaborations and sometimes
   terminate them. ICMJE-style agreement at the outset (and
   written down) avoids the confrontation at the end. The
   conversation is uncomfortable up front and far more
   uncomfortable later; have it early.
